title: The Carmichael Function on Prime Powers: λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻²
description: The parent chain (euler-totient) studies Euler's totient φ. Its OQ-01-OQ-02 asks to prove λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² for k ≥ 3 and related Carmichael (reduced totient) identities. Mathlib defines λ = ArithmeticFunction.Carmichael (the exponent of the unit group (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ) and proves its prime-power values; this entry packages them: λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² = φ(2ᵏ)/2 for k ≥ 3 (non-cyclic ℤ/2 × ℤ/2ᵏ⁻²), λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ) for odd primes (cyclic), λ(n) ∣ φ(n), and concrete λ(8) = 2, λ(16) = 4. 0 axioms.

relatedProblems.relationship: Parent: Euler's totient φ. This entry answers its OQ-01-OQ-02 on the Carmichael (reduced totient) function λ at prime powers.

overview.historicalContext:
The Carmichael function λ(n) is the reduced totient: the smallest positive integer such that a^{λ(n)} ≡ 1 (mod n) for every a coprime to n, i.e. the exponent of the unit group (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ. It always divides Euler's totient φ(n) (the order of that group), but can be strictly smaller when the group is not cyclic. The contrast is sharpest at powers of two: (ℤ/2ℤ)ˣ and (ℤ/4ℤ)ˣ are cyclic, but for k ≥ 3 the group (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ is isomorphic to ℤ/2 × ℤ/2ᵏ⁻², which is not cyclic; its exponent is lcm(2, 2ᵏ⁻²) = 2ᵏ⁻², exactly half of φ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻¹. For odd prime powers the unit group is cyclic, so λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ). Carmichael introduced λ in 1910, and it governs the optimal exponent in Euler's theorem (and the period of decimal/binary expansions, RSA key recovery bounds, etc.).

Mathlib formalizes λ (ArithmeticFunction.Carmichael) as the exponent of (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ and proves its prime-power values, including λ(2ⁿ) = 2ⁿ⁻² for n ≠ 2 and λ(pⁿ) = φ(pⁿ) for odd primes. This entry packages those as the identities the parent's OQ-01-OQ-02 requests.
overview.problemStatement: Prove λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² for k ≥ 3 and related Carmichael identities: that λ(2ᵏ) is half the totient there, that λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ) for odd primes, that λ(n) divides φ(n), the universal-exponent property a^{λ(n)} = 1, and concrete values λ(8) = 2, λ(16) = 4.
overview.proofStrategy: Each identity is the corresponding Mathlib Carmichael theorem restated: carmichael_two_pow = carmichael_two_pow_of_ne_two (k ≥ 3 ⟹ k ≠ 2); two_mul_carmichael_two_pow = two_mul_carmichael_two_pow_of_three_le_eq_totient; carmichael_odd_prime_pow = carmichael_pow_of_prime_ne_two; carmichael_dvd_totient and pow_carmichael are direct. The concrete λ(8), λ(16) instantiate carmichael_two_pow at k = 3, 4 and simplify the powers by norm_num.
keyInsights: λ(n) is the smallest universal exponent — the exponent of (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ — and divides φ(n) (the group order), with equality iff the group is cyclic.
Powers of two are the key non-cyclic case: for k ≥ 3, (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/2ᵏ⁻², so λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² = φ(2ᵏ)/2 — half the totient, the strict-divisor phenomenon made concrete.
Odd prime powers behave oppositely: their unit groups are cyclic, so λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ) and Euler's theorem is already optimal.
The universal-exponent property a^{λ(n)} = 1 is the sharp form of Euler's theorem, with λ(n) often much smaller than φ(n).
The general λ of a composite is the lcm of its prime-power values (Mathlib's carmichael_factorization), so these prime-power identities determine λ everywhere.

sections.title: Overview: The Carmichael Function as the Smallest Universal Exponent
sections.summary: Imports and module docstring. States the parent chain's open question (prove λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² for k ≥ 3 and related Carmichael identities) and explains what λ is: the exponent of the unit group (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ — the SMALLEST k with aᵏ ≡ 1 (mod n) for every unit a, characterized by λ(n) ∣ k. The key structural fact: for n = 2ᵏ (k ≥ 3) the unit group is ℤ/2 × ℤ/2ᵏ⁻² (NOT cyclic), so λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² = φ(2ᵏ)/2 is strictly below φ; for odd prime powers the group is cyclic so λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ). Lists the main results, all packaged from Mathlib's ArithmeticFunction.Carmichael.
sections.mathContext: $\lambda(n) = \exp((\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times)$, the least $k$ with $a^k \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)$ for all units; $\lambda(2^k) = 2^{k-2} = \varphi(2^k)/2$ ($k\ge3$), $\lambda(p^k)=\varphi(p^k)$ for odd $p$.

sections.title: Section I: Powers of Two
sections.summary: carmichael_two_pow (λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² for k ≥ 3, the OQ's target) and two_mul_carmichael_two_pow (2·λ(2ᵏ) = φ(2ᵏ)) — λ is half the totient at high powers of two.
sections.mathContext: The non-cyclic case (ℤ/2 × ℤ/2ᵏ⁻²), where λ is a strict divisor of φ.

sections.title: Section II: Odd Prime Powers and the λ ∣ φ Bound
sections.summary: carmichael_odd_prime_pow records that for an odd prime p the unit group (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic, so λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ); carmichael_dvd_totient gives the always-true divisibility λ(n) ∣ φ(n), the formal statement that λ refines Euler's totient exponent.
sections.mathContext: For odd prime $p$: $(ℤ/p^kℤ)^\times$ cyclic $\Rightarrow \lambda(p^k)=\varphi(p^k)$; in general $\lambda(n)\mid\varphi(n)$.

sections.title: Section III: The Universal Exponent Property
sections.summary: pow_carmichael states the defining property of the Carmichael function: every unit a modulo n satisfies a^{λ(n)} = 1. Combined with λ ∣ φ this makes λ(n) the *smallest* universal exponent, strictly sharper than Euler's a^{φ(n)} = 1 whenever λ(n) < φ(n) (e.g. all 2ᵏ, k ≥ 3).
sections.mathContext: $\forall a\in(ℤ/nℤ)^\times,\ a^{\lambda(n)}=1$, and $\lambda(n)$ is minimal with this property.

sections.title: Section IV: Concrete Values
sections.summary: carmichael_eight (λ(8) = 2) and carmichael_sixteen (λ(16) = 4), instantiating the 2ᵏ formula.

mainTheorems.name: carmichael_two_pow
mainTheorems.description: **λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² for k ≥ 3 — the open question's target.** The unit group (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ is ℤ/2 × ℤ/2ᵏ⁻² (non-cyclic for k ≥ 3), so its exponent is 2ᵏ⁻², strictly smaller than φ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻¹. Packages Mathlib's carmichael_two_pow_of_ne_two.

mainTheorems.name: two_mul_carmichael_two_pow
mainTheorems.description: **λ(2ᵏ) is exactly half the totient**, stated as 2·λ(2ᵏ) = φ(2ᵏ) for k ≥ 3 — the quantitative signature of the non-cyclic ℤ/2 × ℤ/2ᵏ⁻² structure that makes λ strictly smaller than φ.

mainTheorems.name: carmichael_odd_prime_pow
mainTheorems.description: **λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ) for odd primes p.** The unit group of an odd prime power is cyclic, so its exponent equals its order and the Carmichael and totient functions coincide — the contrast case to the powers of two.
mainTheorems.leanType: {p : ℕ} (k : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) (hodd : p ≠ 2) : Carmichael (p ^ k) = (p ^ k).totient

mainTheorems.name: carmichael_dvd_totient
mainTheorems.description: **λ(n) ∣ φ(n).** The Carmichael function always divides the totient: Euler's theorem factors through the smaller universal exponent λ.

mainTheorems.name: pow_carmichael
mainTheorems.description: **Universal exponent property.** Every unit a modulo n satisfies a^{λ(n)} = 1 — the defining property that makes λ(n) a universal exponent for (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ.

mainTheorems.name: carmichael_eight
mainTheorems.description: **λ(8) = 2**, the smallest non-trivial instance of the powers-of-two identity (k = 3), showing the exponent of (ℤ/8ℤ)ˣ ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/2 is 2 while φ(8) = 4.

mainTheorems.name: carmichael_sixteen
mainTheorems.description: **λ(16) = 4** (k = 4): the exponent of (ℤ/16ℤ)ˣ ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/4 is 4 while φ(16) = 8, a second concrete witness of λ(2ᵏ) = φ(2ᵏ)/2.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 75 lines and 7 theorems on the Carmichael function at prime powers: λ(2ᵏ) = 2ᵏ⁻² = φ(2ᵏ)/2 for k ≥ 3 (non-cyclic), λ(pᵏ) = φ(pᵏ) for odd primes (cyclic), λ(n) ∣ φ(n), the universal-exponent property, and λ(8) = 2, λ(16) = 4.
conclusion.implications: This answers the parent's OQ-01-OQ-02, packaging Mathlib's Carmichael prime-power identities. Combined with the lcm formula λ(n) = lcm over prime powers (carmichael_factorization), these determine λ for every n. The result quantifies how far Euler's theorem can be sharpened: the optimal universal exponent λ(n) can be as small as half of φ(n) (powers of two) or equal to it (odd prime powers).
openQuestions: Assemble the full formula λ(n) = lcm of the prime-power values via carmichael_factorization, giving a closed form for arbitrary n.
Formalize an application: the maximal multiplicative order modulo n equals λ(n) when (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ has an element of that order, characterizing the n for which primitive roots exist.
